title: Methodus generalior numeros quosvis satis grandes perscrutandi utrum sint primi necne?

deep.reconstruction: Problem served: deciding by finite computation whether a large N is prime, using representations N = αx² + βy². This page, §§9–15, lays out the theoretical requirements. (§9) The method needs a form with the following property: if N is represented by αx²+βy² in exactly one way (with gcd(x,y)=1 and gcd(N,αβ)=1 understood), then N is prime. Not every form has this property. For 11x²+y², the composite 15 = 11·1²+2² is represented only once. (§10) For any form: if N = αa²+βb² = αA²+βB² in two different ways, put p/q = (a±A)/(b±B) in lowest terms. Then αp²+βq², after removing the small factors α, β, 2, yields a nontrivial factor of N. This is the classical 'two representations ⇒ factorization' device, a gcd/norm argument in Z[√(−αβ)]. (§11) The converse fails for infinitely many forms, so forms where composites can appear only once must be excluded. Euler says he proved elsewhere a rule that separates them. (§12) The rule: set n = αβ. Run through all z coprime to n with n+z² ≤ 4n, i.e. z² ≤ 3n. If every value n+z² is a prime, a square, twice a prime, or a power of 2, the form is 'suitable'. If even one value is composite in any other way, the form is rejected. In modern terms: n is an idoneal number (numerus idoneus), equivalently one class per genus for forms of discriminant −4n (Gauss). (§13) Example n=14 (forms 7x²+2y², 14x²+y²): z = 1, 3, 5 give 15, 23, 39. Both 15 and 39 are composite, so 14 is rejected. (§14) Example n=30: z = 1, 7 give 31 and 79, both prime. So 30x²+y² is accepted, together with the other forms with αβ=30: 15x²+2y², 6x²+5y², 10x²+3y². (§15) Example n=120: z = 1, 7, 11, 13, 17 (19² = 361 > 360). The completion on the next page gives 121, 169, 241, 289, 409, which are primes or squares, so 120 is accepted. All numerical verdicts agree with the known list of idoneal numbers (14 not idoneal; 30 and 120 idoneal).
errors: Euler claims to have 'demonstrated' the rule elsewhere. His criterion was not rigorously proved by him. As stated, allowing 'squares' generally rather than restricting to suitable prime powers, it needed correction and justification, later supplied by Grube (1874). It is also only valid with the coprimality conditions implicit in 'unico modo' (proper representations, gcd(N, αβ)=1).

§9/§11: 'unico modo' is not defined precisely (proper vs improper representations, sign/order conventions, coprimality of N with αβ). The primality statement is only true under these tacit conventions.
§10: the factor rule tacitly requires the two representations to be genuinely distinct and properly primitive. Otherwise (a±A)/(b±B) can give a trivial factor.

ideas.what: If N is represented once (properly) by αx²+βy² with αβ idoneal, then N is prime; used as a primality test
ideas.modern_name: Idoneal numbers / one class per genus primality certificate
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1778 papers, e.g. E708, E715, E719, E725); explained by Gauss, Disquisitiones §303
ideas.where_published: E708, E715, E718/E719, E725 (Nova Acta and Opera postuma); discussed in Weil, Number Theory: an approach through history

ideas.what: Two distinct representations N = αa²+βb² = αA²+βB² give a factor via p/q = (a±A)/(b±B) and αp²+βq²
ideas.modern_name: Euler's factorization method from two representations by a binary quadratic form
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (for sums of two squares, 1740s–1770s; generalized forms here and in related papers)
ideas.where_published: E228 and the 1778 primality papers (E699, E708, E715, etc.)

ideas.what: Finite test: n idoneal iff all n+z² (gcd(z,n)=1, z² ≤ 3n) are p, p² (squares), 2p or 2^k
ideas.where_published: E708, E725 and related Nova Acta papers; Grube, Z. Math. Phys. 19 (1874)

ideas.what: Forms αx²+βy² with the same product αβ share the verdict (e.g. 15x²+2y², 6x²+5y², 10x²+3y² with 30x²+y²)
ideas.modern_name: Diagonal forms of the same discriminant lying in different genera; idoneality depends only on the discriminant
ideas.where_published: Same set of 1778 papers; Gauss DA

deep.surprise_reason: This page is a standard exposition of Euler's idoneal-number criterion and the two-representation factorization trick. Both are well documented and credited to Euler, with Grube's correction known. The examples are correct and match the known idoneal list. Nothing appears to be absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: Transcription is essentially accurate. In §10 the image reads 'Quin etiam haec formula generaliori modo ita exhiberi potest' and the condition is 'per minores divisores α, β, 2'.
§13: 'tanquam ineptam' is the correct reading (the [?] can be removed).
§12: the image reads 'ad productum αβ primi' and 'usque ad terminum 4αβ', consistent with the transcription.
